# Introduction to the Business Problem

A telecom company sells phone and internet plans on monthly bills. Some
customers leave each month. In the industry this is called churn. The
retention department can contact a limited number of customers with an offer,
for example a discount for staying. The department wants to know which
customers to contact first.

The dataset has 7,032 customers and 7 variables. The outcome is `Churn`:
1 if the customer left, 0 if the customer stayed. For each customer we
also know how many months they have been with the company (`tenure`),
the monthly bill in dollars (`MonthlyCharges`), the contract type
(`Contract`), and whether the customer is a senior citizen
(`SeniorCitizen`). Two more variables, `InternetService` and
`PaymentMethod`, are used only in the after-class questions.

The question for the hour is the one from class: how do we turn what we
know about a customer into a probability of churn, how do we read that
model, and how accurate are its predictions on customers it has not
seen?

We will use logistic regression. First we read the coefficients three
ways: as a change in the log-odds, as a multiplier of the odds, and as
a change in the probability. Then we spend most of the hour on
accuracy. On the training customers we read the confusion matrix, the
rates, two thresholds, and a table of thresholds, and we choose one
threshold from that table. Only then do we open the test customers:
the four counts for the threshold we chose, the same two thresholds
again, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, the area
under that curve (AUC), and lift.

Keep the case PDF and the codebook open while you run code. `tenure` is
in months. `MonthlyCharges` is in dollars. A coefficient is only
readable if you know the unit.

**Before you run anything.** The retention department can contact only some
customers. A model gives every customer a probability of churn. What
does the department still have to decide before anyone gets a phone call?
Talk this through with the person next to you. We will come back to it
when we choose the threshold.

# Roadmap

1. **Load the data and code the outcome.** Churn is already 0 and 1.
   Confirm it, and print how common churn is.
2. **Look at churn before any model.** Churn by contract and by tenure.
3. **Hold out 30 percent of the customers.** A stratified split, seed
   467, before the first model.
4. **Estimate the logistic regression on the training customers.**
5. **Read the coefficients three ways.** Log-odds, odds, and
   probability, with two customers we can name.
6. **Marginal effects.** For one customer, then the average over all
   training customers.
7. **Which variables matter most?** One standard deviation of each, and
   what happens when a variable is dropped. Skip the second chunk if
   the hour is short.
8. **Score the training customers.** One probability per customer.
   The test customers stay closed.
9. **From a probability to a predicted churner.** The threshold, on
   the training customers.
10. **The confusion matrix at 0.50.** Training customers.
11. **Four rates.** Sensitivity, specificity, precision, and the
    false-positive rate.
12. **A lower threshold: 0.30, and the training threshold table.**
    This is the table you choose from.
13. **Commit to one threshold.** From that table only. No test counts
    yet.
14. **Report it on the test customers.** Your four test counts on the
    board, and 0.50 and 0.30 on the test customers for comparison.
15. **Every threshold at once.** The ROC curve and the area under it
    (AUC), test against training, once.
16. **Who gets the offer first?** Lift and the gains chart, on the
    test customers.
17. **After class.** The straight-line model, internet service and the
    monthly bill, payment method, a threshold from example costs, a
    second seed, and a model with the bill only.

# 1. Load the data and code the outcome

```{r}
#| label: setup
# rsample: initial_split() makes the training and test sets.
# marginaleffects: slopes(), avg_slopes(), and avg_comparisons() turn
#   coefficients into changes in the probability.
# ggplot2 and scales: plots.
# This chunk stops if a package is missing. It does not install anything.
needed <- c("rsample", "marginaleffects", "ggplot2", "scales")
missing <- needed[!vapply(needed, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Install the missing packages in the Console, then render again:\n",
    "install.packages(c(",
    paste0('"', missing, '"', collapse = ", "), "))"
  )
}

library(rsample)
library(marginaleffects)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
churn <- read.csv("data/churn.csv")

# Contract and SeniorCitizen become factors so the dummy coding is
# explicit. Month-to-month is the first level, so it is the reference:
# the One year and Two year coefficients compare with month-to-month
# customers. SeniorCitizen is 0/1 in the csv. As a factor, R reports
# the senior coefficient as SeniorCitizenYes.
churn$Contract <- factor(churn$Contract,
                         levels = c("Month-to-month", "One year", "Two year"))
churn$SeniorCitizen <- factor(churn$SeniorCitizen, levels = c(0, 1),
                              labels = c("No", "Yes"))
# Internet service and payment method are for the after-class questions.
# Code them now, before the split, so training and test use the same
# levels. Do not put them in the model during the hour.
churn$InternetService <- factor(churn$InternetService)
churn$PaymentMethod <- factor(churn$PaymentMethod)

str(churn)
class_vars <- c("Churn", "tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "Contract", "SeniorCitizen")
summary(churn[class_vars])
sum(is.na(churn))

# The outcome must be 0/1 with the event we care about coded 1.
# Here the event is churn.
table(churn$Churn)
mean(churn$Churn)

# Question: How many customers churned, and what share is that?
#
# Interpret: glm() models the probability that the outcome is 1. Since
# churn is 1, every probability in this lab is a probability of churn.
#
# Discuss: Suppose a manager says "we predict that nobody churns." How
# often would that prediction be correct in this dataset? Keep that
# number. It is the benchmark for accuracy later.
```

# 2. Look at churn before any model

```{r}
#| label: churn-by-group
# Share of customers who churned, by contract type and by senior status.
tapply(churn$Churn, churn$Contract, mean)
table(churn$Contract)
tapply(churn$Churn, churn$SeniorCitizen, mean)

# Tenure in one-year groups.
churn$tenure_group <- cut(churn$tenure, breaks = c(0, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72),
                          labels = c("1-12", "13-24", "25-36",
                                     "37-48", "49-60", "61-72"))
tenure_share <- data.frame(
  group = levels(churn$tenure_group),
  share = as.numeric(tapply(churn$Churn, churn$tenure_group, mean))
)
tenure_share

# Question: Which contract type churns most? By how many percentage
# points does it differ from a two-year contract?
#
# Discuss: These are shares inside groups. A new customer arrives with
# a tenure, a bill, a contract, and senior-citizen status all at once. Why do we
# need a model, and not only these tables?
```

```{r}
#| label: tenure-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
ggplot(tenure_share, aes(x = group, y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#156082", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(
    x = "Tenure (months)",
    y = "Share who churned",
    title = paste("Churn by tenure group, all",
                  format(nrow(churn), big.mark = ","), "customers")
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Interpret: The share falls as tenure grows, and it does not fall by
# the same amount in each step. A straight line in tenure would not
# follow these bars. The logistic curve can bend.
```

# 3. Hold out 30 percent of the customers

```{r}
#| label: split
# Stratified 70/30 split. strata = Churn keeps the churn share almost
# the same in the training and test sets.
# Why before the first model? If we read the test customers while we
# build the model or choose a threshold, the test is no longer a test.
set.seed(467)
churn_split <- initial_split(churn, prop = 0.7, strata = Churn)
train <- training(churn_split)
test <- testing(churn_split)

nrow(train)
nrow(test)
mean(train$Churn)
mean(test$Churn)

# Question: Why do the two churn shares match so closely? What could go
# wrong with a plain random split if churn were rare, say 3 percent?
#
# From here on: coefficients are read on `train`. The threshold is
# chosen from the training probabilities. The four counts you report
# are computed on `test`, after that choice.
```

# 4. Estimate the logistic regression on the training customers

The model gives a score for each customer. The score is a line in the
variables. The logistic curve turns the score into a probability
between 0 and 1:

$$
\text{score} = b_0 + b_1\,\text{tenure} + b_2\,\text{MonthlyCharges}
+ b_3\,\text{OneYear} + b_4\,\text{TwoYear} + b_5\,\text{Senior},
\qquad
p = \frac{e^{\text{score}}}{1 + e^{\text{score}}}.
$$

The score is the log-odds of churn: $\log\big(p / (1 - p)\big)$.
`OneYear`, `TwoYear`, and `Senior` are 0/1 indicators. A month-to-month
customer has `OneYear = 0` and `TwoYear = 0`.

```{r}
#| label: glm
churn_model <- glm(Churn ~ tenure + MonthlyCharges + Contract + SeniorCitizen,
                   data = train, family = binomial)
summary(churn_model)
round(coef(churn_model), 4)

# Question: Read only the signs. Which variables go with a higher
# probability of churn, and which with a lower one?
#
# Question: The intercept is the score for a customer with tenure 0, a
# $0 bill, a month-to-month contract, and not a senior. Does that
# customer exist in this dataset? Check the minimum of tenure and of
# MonthlyCharges in the summary above.
#
# Interpret: ContractOne year and ContractTwo year are each compared
# with month-to-month, the reference level. They are not compared with
# each other.
```

# 5. Read the coefficients three ways

Each coefficient has three readings. In log-odds it adds a fixed amount
to the score. In odds it multiplies the odds by a fixed factor. In
probability the change depends on where the customer starts.

Use a step a customer can actually take. One extra month of tenure, or
one extra dollar on the bill, is too small to talk about. We use 12
months and $10.

```{r}
#| label: odds-steps
b <- coef(churn_model)

# Log-odds change for a realistic step.
c(tenure_12_months = 12 * b[["tenure"]],
  charges_10_dollars = 10 * b[["MonthlyCharges"]])

# Odds multiplier: e to that change. Below 1 means lower odds of churn.
round(c(tenure_12_months = exp(12 * b[["tenure"]]),
        charges_10_dollars = exp(10 * b[["MonthlyCharges"]]),
        one_year_vs_month = exp(b[["ContractOne year"]]),
        two_year_vs_month = exp(b[["ContractTwo year"]]),
        senior_vs_not = exp(b[["SeniorCitizenYes"]])), 3)

# Question: Write one sentence for tenure in odds: "Holding the bill,
# the contract, and senior status fixed, 12 more months of tenure
# multiplies the odds of churn by ___." Then say it as a percent change
# in the odds.
#
# Discuss: An odds multiplier of 0.5 and a probability that falls by
# half are not the same thing. Why not?
```

Now two customers we can name. Both pay $80 a month and are not senior
citizens.

- **Customer A:** 6 months of tenure, month-to-month contract.
- **Customer B:** 36 months of tenure, one-year contract.

```{r}
#| label: two-customers
customers <- data.frame(
  customer = c("A", "B"),
  tenure = c(6, 36),
  MonthlyCharges = c(80, 80),
  Contract = factor(c("Month-to-month", "One year"), levels = levels(churn$Contract)),
  SeniorCitizen = factor(c("No", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
)

# Score by hand from the coefficients. A is month-to-month, so no
# contract term. B adds the One year coefficient.
score_A <- b[["(Intercept)"]] + b[["tenure"]] * 6 + b[["MonthlyCharges"]] * 80
score_B <- b[["(Intercept)"]] + b[["tenure"]] * 36 + b[["MonthlyCharges"]] * 80 +
  b[["ContractOne year"]]
p_hand <- exp(c(score_A, score_B)) / (1 + exp(c(score_A, score_B)))

# The same probabilities from predict(). type = "response" returns the
# probability. Without it, predict() returns the score.
p_now <- predict(churn_model, customers, type = "response")
round(data.frame(score = c(score_A, score_B), p_hand, p_predict = p_now), 4)

# Question: What is each customer's probability of churn? Do the hand
# calculation and predict() agree?
```

```{r}
#| label: same-step-two-customers
# Give both customers 12 more months of tenure. Then, separately, $10
# more on the bill. Everything else stays the same.
plus_12 <- customers
plus_12$tenure <- plus_12$tenure + 12
plus_10 <- customers
plus_10$MonthlyCharges <- plus_10$MonthlyCharges + 10

p_12 <- predict(churn_model, plus_12, type = "response")
p_10 <- predict(churn_model, plus_10, type = "response")
odds <- function(p) p / (1 - p)

data.frame(
  customer = customers$customer,
  p_now = round(p_now, 3),
  p_12_more_months = round(p_12, 3),
  change_pp = round(100 * (p_12 - p_now), 1),
  odds_ratio = round(odds(p_12) / odds(p_now), 3),
  p_10_more_dollars = round(p_10, 3),
  change_pp_bill = round(100 * (p_10 - p_now), 1)
)

# Interpret: change_pp is in percentage points. Going from 0.40 to
# 0.30 is 10 percentage points, and it is a 25 percent drop. Say
# "percentage points" when you mean the first.
#
# Question: The odds ratio is the same for A and B. The change in
# percentage points is not. Which customer moves more, and why?
```

```{r}
#| label: contract-before-after
# A category is read as a before-and-after difference. Keep customer A
# the same, and change only the contract.
a_contracts <- customers[c(1, 1, 1), ]
a_contracts$Contract <- factor(c("Month-to-month", "One year", "Two year"),
                               levels = levels(churn$Contract))
data.frame(contract = a_contracts$Contract,
           p_churn = round(predict(churn_model, a_contracts, type = "response"), 3))

# Question: By how many percentage points does customer A's probability
# fall if A were on a one-year contract instead of month-to-month? On a
# two-year contract?
#
# Interpret: This compares customers who have different contracts. It
# does not say that switching A to a two-year contract would cause that
# drop. Customers who sign two-year contracts may differ in ways the
# model does not see.
```

# 6. Marginal effects: for one customer, then the average

The marginal effect of a numeric variable is how fast the probability
moves when that variable moves, at a given customer:

$$
\text{marginal effect of } x_j = b_j \times p \times (1 - p).
$$

It uses that customer's $p$, so it is different for every customer.
The average marginal effect (AME) is the average of the marginal
effects of all training customers, each at its own $p$.

```{r}
#| label: me-one-customer
# By hand: coefficient times p(1 - p), for customers A and B.
p_A <- p_now[[1]]
p_B <- p_now[[2]]
c(tenure_A = b[["tenure"]] * p_A * (1 - p_A),
  tenure_B = b[["tenure"]] * p_B * (1 - p_B))

# The same numbers from marginaleffects. slopes() returns the marginal
# effect at each customer in newdata. We print the customer, the
# variable, the estimate, and the standard error.
me_customers <- slopes(churn_model, newdata = customers,
                       variables = c("tenure", "MonthlyCharges"))
as.data.frame(me_customers)[, c("customer", "term", "estimate", "std.error")]

# Interpret: The estimate is the change for one extra month of tenure,
# or one extra dollar of bill, at that customer's current probability.
#
# Question: For customer A, how many percentage points does one more
# month of tenure change the probability of churn? Is that close to
# one-twelfth of the 12-month change you computed above? Why is it not
# exactly one-twelfth?
```

```{r}
#| label: ame
# Average marginal effect, by hand: one marginal effect per training
# customer, then the average.
p_train <- predict(churn_model, type = "response")
c(tenure = mean(b[["tenure"]] * p_train * (1 - p_train)),
  MonthlyCharges = mean(b[["MonthlyCharges"]] * p_train * (1 - p_train)))

# The same averages from marginaleffects. In the printed tables, S is
# another way to show the p-value. We do not use it today.
avg_slopes(churn_model, variables = c("tenure", "MonthlyCharges"))

# The average change for the realistic steps: 12 months and $10.
avg_comparisons(churn_model, variables = list(tenure = 12, MonthlyCharges = 10))

# For the categories, avg_comparisons() changes each training customer
# from the reference level to the other level, and averages the
# before-and-after difference.
avg_comparisons(churn_model, variables = c("Contract", "SeniorCitizen"))

# Question: Report the average effect of 12 more months of tenure in
# percentage points. Is it larger or smaller than customer A's change?
# Than customer B's?
#
# Discuss: For a category, why do we compute the probability before and
# after, instead of multiplying the coefficient by p(1 - p)? Try it for
# customer A and the two-year contract, and compare with the
# contract-before-after chunk.
#
# Discuss: One number is the change for customer A. The other is the
# average over the training customers. Which one answers a question
# about customer A, and which one answers a question about every
# customer?
```

# 7. Which variables matter most?

Coefficients are per unit, and the units differ: months, dollars, and
categories. A larger coefficient does not mean a more important
variable. A very small p-value does not mean that either. It means an
estimate this far from zero would be rare if the coefficient were zero.
For the two numeric variables,
multiply each coefficient by its standard deviation. That is the change
in the log-odds for a typical difference between customers.

```{r}
#| label: importance-sd
sds <- c(tenure = sd(train$tenure), MonthlyCharges = sd(train$MonthlyCharges))
b_num <- b[c("tenure", "MonthlyCharges")]
std <- b_num * sds
round(rbind(coefficient = b_num, sd = sds, log_odds_per_sd = std,
            odds_per_sd = exp(std)), 3)

# Question: In odds, which moves churn more: one standard deviation of
# tenure or one standard deviation of the monthly bill? How do you
# compare a multiplier below 1 with one above 1? (Hint: 1 / multiplier.)
```

```{r}
#| label: importance-drop1
# Skip this chunk if the hour is short.
# drop1() estimates the model again without each variable and reports
# the deviance. Deviance measures how far the probabilities are from
# the outcomes. Lower is better. A large increase means the model
# needs that variable. This works for Contract
# too, which has no single standard deviation.
drop1(churn_model, test = "LRT")

# Question: Which variable's removal hurts the model most? Which
# hurts it least? Do all four stay?
```

# 8. Score the training customers

The test customers stay closed until the threshold is chosen. Every
number in the next sections is a training customer. The model was
estimated on these same customers, so the counts here are for choosing,
not for the board.

```{r}
#| label: score-train
train$p_churn <- predict(churn_model, type = "response")
summary(train$p_churn)

# Sort the training customers from the highest probability to the lowest.
ranked <- train[order(train$p_churn, decreasing = TRUE),
                c("tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "Contract", "SeniorCitizen",
                  "p_churn", "Churn")]
head(ranked, 5)
tail(ranked, 5)

# Question: What do the five customers at the top of the list have in
# common? And the five at the bottom? Look at tenure, the bill, the
# contract, and whether they actually churned.
```

# 9. From a probability to a predicted churner: the threshold

A probability is not yet a decision. The retention department needs a list.
We choose a threshold (some books say cutoff) and predict churn when
the probability is above it.

We look at two thresholds on the training customers. The usual default
is 0.50. The second is 0.30. Compare the mistakes each one makes.
You will choose one threshold from the training table. The test
customers stay closed until that choice is made.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-hist
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
train$outcome <- factor(ifelse(train$Churn == 1, "Churned", "Stayed"),
                        levels = c("Churned", "Stayed"))
ggplot(train, aes(x = p_churn)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, boundary = 0, fill = "#156082", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.50, color = "#C41230", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.30, color = "#e97132", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted probability of churn (training customers)",
    y = "Customers",
    title = "Training customers by what they actually did",
    subtitle = "Red line: threshold 0.50. Orange dashed line: threshold 0.30. Right of a line = predicted to churn."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

c(above_0.50 = sum(train$p_churn > 0.50), above_0.30 = sum(train$p_churn > 0.30))

# Question: The red line is the 0.50 threshold. Do the two panels sit
# on opposite sides of it, or do they overlap?
#
# Interpret: Where the panels overlap, every threshold makes mistakes.
# A churner left of the line is predicted to stay. A customer who
# stayed and sits right of the line is predicted to churn.
```

# 10. The confusion matrix at 0.50

These counts are the training customers. They show how the table works.
They are not the counts that go on the board.

The positive class is the one we want to find: here, churn. The
prediction runs down the left side of the table; what the customer
actually did runs across the top.

|   | Actually churned | Actually stayed |
|---|---|---|
| **Predicted churn** | True positive (TP) | False positive (FP), Type I error |
| **Predicted stay** | False negative (FN), Type II error | True negative (TN) |

A false positive is a customer we contact who would have stayed anyway.
A false negative is a churner we miss.

```{r}
#| label: confusion-050
predicted <- factor(ifelse(train$p_churn > 0.50, "Churn", "Stay"),
                    levels = c("Churn", "Stay"))
actual <- factor(ifelse(train$Churn == 1, "Churn", "Stay"),
                 levels = c("Churn", "Stay"))
cm_050 <- table(predicted, actual)
cm_050

# Accuracy: the share of all training customers predicted correctly.
accuracy_050 <- sum(diag(cm_050)) / sum(cm_050)
# Benchmark: predict that nobody churns.
nobody <- mean(train$Churn == 0)
round(c(model_0.50 = accuracy_050, predict_nobody_churns = nobody), 3)

# Question: Read the four training counts. How many training customers
# would the department contact at 0.50? How many of them churned? How
# many churners are missed?
#
# Question: How many percentage points does the model add over
# "nobody churns"? How many churners does "nobody churns" find?
#
# Discuss: Accuracy treats a missed churner and an unneeded call as
# the same mistake. Are they the same for this company?
```

# 11. Four rates

Each rate divides by a different group. Before you read a rate, ask: a
share of which customers?

- **Sensitivity** (also called recall): of the customers who churned,
  the share we flagged. TP / (TP + FN).
- **Specificity**: of the customers who stayed, the share we did not
  flag. TN / (TN + FP).
- **Precision**: of the customers we flagged, the share who churned.
  TP / (TP + FP).
- **False-positive rate**: of the customers who stayed, the share we
  flagged. FP / (FP + TN), which is 1 − specificity.

```{r}
#| label: rates
# Counts and rates for any threshold, on the training customers.
# This is the table the threshold is chosen from.
counts <- function(threshold) {
  flag <- train$p_churn > threshold
  c(TP = sum(flag & train$Churn == 1), FP = sum(flag & train$Churn == 0),
    FN = sum(!flag & train$Churn == 1), TN = sum(!flag & train$Churn == 0))
}
rates <- function(threshold) {
  k <- counts(threshold)
  c(accuracy = unname((k["TP"] + k["TN"]) / sum(k)),
    sensitivity = unname(k["TP"] / (k["TP"] + k["FN"])),
    specificity = unname(k["TN"] / (k["TN"] + k["FP"])),
    precision = unname(k["TP"] / (k["TP"] + k["FP"])),
    false_positive_rate = unname(k["FP"] / (k["FP"] + k["TN"])))
}
counts(0.50)
round(rates(0.50), 3)

# Question: At 0.50, what share of churners does the list catch? Say
# it in a sentence a manager would understand.
#
# Question: Precision and sensitivity both have TP on top. What is
# different about the bottom of each fraction?
#
# Discuss: Recall asks how many churners we found. Precision asks how
# many of the customers we flagged really churned. If the department
# can make only a few calls, which one matters more?
```

# 12. A lower threshold: 0.30

```{r}
#| label: threshold-030
rbind(threshold_0.50 = counts(0.50), threshold_0.30 = counts(0.30))
round(rbind(threshold_0.50 = rates(0.50), threshold_0.30 = rates(0.30)), 3)

# Question: On the training customers, moving from 0.50 to 0.30, how
# many more churners does the list catch? How many more customers who
# would have stayed does it contact?
#
# Question: Compare accuracy at 0.30 with accuracy at 0.50. Does a
# lower accuracy make 0.30 the worse threshold for the retention
# department?
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-table
# The list at several thresholds, so you can see it move.
threshold_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq(0.1, 0.8, by = 0.1), function(k) {
  cc <- counts(k)
  data.frame(threshold = k, contacted = cc[["TP"]] + cc[["FP"]],
             TP = cc[["TP"]], FP = cc[["FP"]], FN = cc[["FN"]], TN = cc[["TN"]],
             t(round(rates(k), 3)))
}))
threshold_table

# Interpret: Read the contacted numbers from 0.10 down to 0.80. Every
# time the threshold moves, the list changes.
#
# Question: Look at threshold 0.80. Why is the list so short? What is
# the highest predicted probability among the training customers?
```

**Before you commit.** The table above is the training customers. Talk
with the person next to you. Which mistake is worse for this company:
calling a customer who would have stayed, or missing a churner? How
many customers can a retention department realistically contact? No
dollar figures. Do not open the test customers to make this choice.

In class, the lowest-cost threshold was $c_{FP} / (c_{FP} + c_{FN})$:
the cost of a false positive over the sum of the two costs. You only
need the ratio. If a missed churner costs about twice as much as an
unneeded call, the rule gives $1 / (1 + 2) = 0.33$. Three times as
much gives $1 / (1 + 3) = 0.25$.

# 13. Commit to one threshold

Choose a threshold from the training table. A row in the table is fine.
A value between two rows is fine if you can defend it.

Write it in the next chunk, then run it. The counts it prints are the
training counts: the trade-off you are choosing. They do not go on the
board. The four board counts are the test counts, in the chunk after
this one.

The line below is a starting point so the document renders. Replace it
with the threshold you chose.

```{r}
#| label: commit
# Starting point only, so the chunk runs. Replace this line.
# counts() uses the training customers.
my_threshold <- 0.50

my_counts <- counts(my_threshold)
my_threshold
my_counts
c(contacted = my_counts[["TP"]] + my_counts[["FP"]],
  churners_caught = my_counts[["TP"]],
  churners_missed = my_counts[["FN"]],
  calls_to_customers_who_stayed = my_counts[["FP"]])
round(rates(my_threshold), 3)

# Discuss: Picking the training row with the highest accuracy treats a
# missed churner and an unneeded call as the same mistake. Opening the
# test customers to pick the threshold would mean the test set is no
# longer a test. What are you using to choose instead?
#
# Interpret: The threshold is a choice about the two mistakes. The model
# ranks customers. It does not decide how many to call.
```

# 14. Report the threshold on the test customers

The threshold is chosen. Open the test customers once. On the board,
write your threshold, its four test counts (TP, FP, FN, TN), and one
or two sentences on why. No dollar figures.

The same chunk prints 0.50 and 0.30 on the test customers, so the two
reference thresholds can be compared on customers the choice did not
use.

```{r}
#| label: report-test
# The threshold is already chosen. Do not change my_threshold
# after reading these test counts.
test$p_churn <- predict(churn_model, test, type = "response")

test_counts <- function(threshold) {
  flag <- test$p_churn > threshold
  c(TP = sum(flag & test$Churn == 1), FP = sum(flag & test$Churn == 0),
    FN = sum(!flag & test$Churn == 1), TN = sum(!flag & test$Churn == 0))
}
test_rates <- function(threshold) {
  k <- test_counts(threshold)
  c(accuracy = unname((k["TP"] + k["TN"]) / sum(k)),
    sensitivity = unname(k["TP"] / (k["TP"] + k["FN"])),
    specificity = unname(k["TN"] / (k["TN"] + k["FP"])),
    precision = unname(k["TP"] / (k["TP"] + k["FP"])),
    false_positive_rate = unname(k["FP"] / (k["FP"] + k["TN"])))
}

my_test <- test_counts(my_threshold)
my_threshold
my_test
c(contacted = my_test[["TP"]] + my_test[["FP"]],
  churners_caught = my_test[["TP"]],
  churners_missed = my_test[["FN"]],
  calls_to_customers_who_stayed = my_test[["FP"]])

rbind(chosen = test_counts(my_threshold),
      threshold_0.50 = test_counts(0.50),
      threshold_0.30 = test_counts(0.30))
round(rbind(chosen = test_rates(my_threshold),
            threshold_0.50 = test_rates(0.50),
            threshold_0.30 = test_rates(0.30),
            nobody = c(accuracy = mean(test$Churn == 0),
                       sensitivity = 0, specificity = 1,
                       precision = NA, false_positive_rate = 0)), 3)

# Question: Read your four test counts. How many test customers would
# the department contact? How many of them churned? How many churners
# are missed?
#
# Question: At your threshold, how does test accuracy compare with
# "nobody churns" on the test customers? How many churners does
# "nobody churns" find?
```

# 15. Every threshold at once: the ROC curve and the area under it

The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots, for every
threshold, the false-positive rate on the horizontal axis and the
sensitivity (true-positive rate) on the vertical axis. Each threshold
is one point.

The area under the curve (AUC) has two readings, as in class.

- **How high the curve is.** The AUC is the average share of churners
  found, over all false-positive rates. A higher curve finds more
  churners at every level of false alarms.
- **Pairs.** Pick one customer who churned and one who stayed, at
  random. The AUC is the probability that the model gives the churner
  the higher probability of churn. 0.5 is a coin toss. 1 is perfect.

```{r}
#| label: roc
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6
# One point per threshold, as in class: 101 thresholds from 0 to 1.
thresholds <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
# fpr: share of the customers who stayed that are flagged.
# tpr: share of the churners that are flagged.
roc_test <- data.frame(
  fpr = sapply(thresholds, function(k) mean(test$p_churn[test$Churn == 0] > k)),
  tpr = sapply(thresholds, function(k) mean(test$p_churn[test$Churn == 1] > k))
)

# The AUC as pairs, the function from class.
auc_of <- function(p, y) {                               # pairs ranked right
  ch <- p[y == 1]; st <- p[y == 0]                       # churners and stayers
  mean(outer(ch, st, ">") + 0.5 * outer(ch, st, "=="))   # ties count half
}
auc_test <- auc_of(test$p_churn, test$Churn)
# In practice, yardstick::roc_auc() gives the same AUC in one line.

two_points <- data.frame(
  fpr = c(test_rates(0.50)[["false_positive_rate"]],
          test_rates(0.30)[["false_positive_rate"]]),
  tpr = c(test_rates(0.50)[["sensitivity"]],
          test_rates(0.30)[["sensitivity"]]),
  label = c("threshold 0.50", "threshold 0.30")
)

your_point <- data.frame(
  fpr = test_rates(my_threshold)[["false_positive_rate"]],
  tpr = test_rates(my_threshold)[["sensitivity"]],
  label = paste("your threshold,", my_threshold)
)

ggplot(roc_test, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr)) +
  geom_path(color = "#156082", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = two_points, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr), color = "#C41230", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = two_points, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, label = label),
            hjust = -0.15, vjust = 1.3, color = "#C41230") +
  geom_point(data = your_point, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr),
             color = "#e97132", size = 4, shape = 17) +
  geom_text(data = your_point, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, label = label),
            hjust = -0.15, vjust = 2.9, color = "#e97132") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "False-positive rate (1 - specificity)",
    y = "Sensitivity (true-positive rate)",
    title = "ROC curve, test customers",
    subtitle = paste0("AUC: ", round(auc_test, 3),
                      ". Dashed line: random guessing. Triangle: your threshold.")
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

round(c(AUC = auc_test, gini = 2 * auc_test - 1), 3)

# Question: Moving from 0.50 to 0.30, which way does the point move on
# the curve? Why do both rates rise?
#
# Question: Say the area under the curve in one sentence about a
# churner and a customer who stayed.
#
# Interpret: The Gini coefficient here is 2 times the area, minus 1.
# Random guessing is 0 and a perfect ranking is 1. This is not the
# Gini measure of income inequality. Some industries report this
# Gini instead of the area.
```

```{r}
#| label: auc-train-vs-test
# Once. The training probabilities were used to choose the threshold.
# This is the one comparison with the test area.
auc_train <- auc_of(train$p_churn, train$Churn)
round(c(training = auc_train, test = auc_test), 3)

# Question: Is the test area much lower than the training area? What
# does that say about overfitting with four variables?
#
# Discuss: The area does not choose a threshold. What is it useful for?
```

# 16. Who gets the offer first? Lift and the gains chart

The threshold is already chosen. This chart does not pick a new one.
The department may have budget for only part of the list. Sort the test
customers by probability of churn, highest first, and contact from the
top. Lift in the top 10 percent is the churn share in that slice
divided by the churn share among all test customers.

```{r}
#| label: lift
o <- order(test$p_churn, decreasing = TRUE)
churned_sorted <- test$Churn[o]
n_top <- round(0.10 * nrow(test))

round(c(customers_in_top_10 = n_top,
        churners_in_top_10 = sum(churned_sorted[1:n_top]),
        share_top_10 = mean(churned_sorted[1:n_top]),
        share_all = mean(churned_sorted),
        lift_top_10 = mean(churned_sorted[1:n_top]) / mean(churned_sorted),
        share_of_churners_reached = sum(churned_sorted[1:n_top]) / sum(churned_sorted)), 3)

# Question: If the department contacted the same number of customers at
# random, about how many churners would it reach? How many does the
# model's top 10 percent reach?
#
# Discuss: Suppose the offer works best on customers who have not
# made up their mind yet. Would you call the top of this list first,
# or further down? What would you need to know?
```

```{r}
#| label: gains
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
gains <- data.frame(
  share_contacted = c(0, seq_along(churned_sorted) / length(churned_sorted)),
  share_churners = c(0, cumsum(churned_sorted) / sum(churned_sorted))
)
ggplot(gains, aes(x = share_contacted, y = share_churners)) +
  geom_line(color = "#156082", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.1, 0.3), color = "#e97132", linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    x = "Share of test customers contacted, highest probability first",
    y = "Share of test churners reached",
    title = "Gains chart, test customers",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: contacting customers at random. Dotted lines: top 10% and top 30%."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

n_30 <- round(0.30 * length(churned_sorted))
round(c(top_30_customers = n_30,
        share_of_churners_reached =
          sum(churned_sorted[seq_len(n_30)]) / sum(churned_sorted)), 3)

# Question: Contacting 30 percent of the test customers at random would
# reach about 30 percent of the churners, on average. What share does
# the top 30 percent of this list reach, and how does it compare?
#
# Discuss: Lift looks only at the top of the list. The confusion matrix
# looks at one threshold. The ROC curve looks at all thresholds. Which
# one helps a department with a fixed number of calls?
```

```{r}
#| label: after-class-costs
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
# EXAMPLE numbers. They are not in the dataset. Change them.
offer_cost <- 50      # dollars per customer contacted
value_kept <- 300     # dollars, value of a churner who stays
accept_share <- 0.5   # share of contacted churners who accept and stay

break_even <- offer_cost / (accept_share * value_kept)
break_even

profit_on <- function(count_fn, threshold) {
  k <- count_fn(threshold)
  k[["TP"]] * accept_share * value_kept - (k[["TP"]] + k[["FP"]]) * offer_cost
}
grid <- seq(0.05, 0.80, by = 0.01)
profit_grid <- data.frame(
  threshold = grid,
  profit = sapply(grid, function(k) profit_on(counts, k))
)
chosen_cost <- profit_grid$threshold[which.max(profit_grid$profit)]
chosen_cost
c(test_at_chosen = profit_on(test_counts, chosen_cost),
  test_at_0.50 = profit_on(test_counts, 0.50),
  test_at_0.30 = profit_on(test_counts, 0.30))

ggplot(profit_grid, aes(threshold, profit)) +
  geom_line(color = "#156082", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = break_even, color = "#e97132", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = chosen_cost, color = "#C41230", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Threshold", y = "Profit on training customers (EXAMPLE costs)",
       title = "Example profit by threshold, training customers",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: break-even probability. Red line: threshold chosen on the training customers.") +
  theme_minimal()
```
